Year 9 Enquiry • 1914–1919

The Great War: 1914–1919

Industrial Slaughter, Global Sacrifice, Total War & The Flawed Peace
The Signing of Peace in the Hall of Mirrors, Versailles (28 June 1919) Sir William Orpen (1878–1931)

On 28 June 1919, exactly five years after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Allied statesmen gathered in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles to impose peace upon defeated Germany:

1. The Big Three & Conflicting Agendas:
Seated at the centre are Woodrow Wilson (League of Nations), Georges Clemenceau (disarmament and reparations), and David Lloyd George (imperial compromise).
2. The Imposition of the Diktat:
In the foreground, German envoys Johannes Bell and Hermann Müller sign Article 231 (War Guilt) and £6.6bn in reparations without negotiation under naval blockade.
3. Global Imperial Representation:
Flanked behind the leaders stand imperial dignitaries—including the Maharaja of Bikaner—symbolising over 4 million colonial troops who sustained Allied victory.
4. The Seeds of Future Conflict:
Above, the ceiling proclaims ‘Le Roy Gouverne’ (‘The King Governs’), foreshadowing Marshal Foch’s warning: ‘This is not peace. It is an armistice for twenty years.’
The Big Three
Wilson, Clemenceau, Lloyd George.
German Envoys
Signing Article 231 (War Guilt).
Hall of Mirrors
1871 German Empire reversed.
Significance: The Treaty of Versailles formally concluded the Great War, dismantled four European empires, and created the economic and territorial grievances that paved the road to the Second World War.
Hinge Question:
Did the Allied peacemakers at Versailles make another war inevitable through excessive severity, or was the fatal weakness their failure to enforce the treaty’s military terms when challenged in the 1930s?
Medium & Provenance: Oil on canvas (152.4 × 127 cm) • Official War Art Commission IMPERIAL WAR MUSEUM, LONDON • ART 2856

In 1914, Britain was the only major European power without peacetime conscription, relying entirely on voluntary enlistment. 1/16
ENQUIRY 1 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 9 • THE GREAT WAR: 1914–1919

Why were young British men so desperate to volunteer for the slaughter of 1914?

Core Specification Focus: Lack of peacetime conscription; Lord Kitchener’s recruitment campaign; moral outrage over the invasion of neutral Belgium; Pals Battalions (Pompey Pals); economic poverty & the King’s Shilling; propaganda posters & White Feather shame.

Enquiry Writing Task [8 marks • 10 mins]

HISTORIOGRAPHICAL ANALYSIS
Interpretation 1 • Lord Curzon, British War Cabinet Minister, Speech at the Royal Albert Hall (1917)
“The Indian Army and the troops from our dominions have rushed forward with magnificent devotion to defend the King-Emperor. Side by side with their British brothers-in-arms, they have shed their blood on the plains of Flanders, Gallipoli, and Egypt. This imperial brotherhood proves that the British Empire is held together not by force, but by mutual love, loyalty, and common sacrifice.”
Interpretation 2 • David Olusoga, Modern British Historian, The World’s War (2014)
“Over four million non-white men were mobilised as combatants and labourers by Britain. Yet their treatment was defined by systemic racism. Black and Asian soldiers were barred from becoming officers, paid a fraction of British wages, and subjected to brutal floggings. After 1918, the Imperial War Graves Commission deliberately refused to give African dead individual headstones. Their sacrifice was whitewashed from British national memory.”
Task A: Explain how Interpretations 1 and 2 differ about the experiences of colonial troops in the Great War. [4 marks]
PART B
Sentence Stems: Interpretation 1 emphasizes that colonial troops were treated with... • In contrast, Interpretation 2 argues that their service was characterized by... • Specifically, Interpretation 1 claims... whereas Interpretation 2 reveals...
Task B: Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 differ about the role of empire soldiers. [4 marks]
PART C
Scaffolded Sentence Stems: One reason why the interpretations differ is because the authors have different perspectives and purposes. The author of Interpretation 1 was writing from the perspective of... with the purpose of... • On the other hand, the author of Interpretation 2 is evaluating the events from the perspective of... • Consequently, this shaped their conclusions because...

Living Timeline • Part 1: Enlistment, Empire Mobilisation & The Somme (1914–1916)

Living Timeline Dual-Coding Protocol: Complete each milestone sketchpad using dual-coding (combining visual storytelling symbols, causal arrows, and dates) to master the chronological spine across the centre-fold.
August 1914 • The Rush to the Colours & Lord Kitchener’s Appeal Enquiry 1

Following the German invasion of Belgium, Lord Kitchener issues his iconic recruiting appeal; over 750,000 volunteers enlist in eight weeks, creating the civic Pals Battalions across Britain.

April 1915 • The Gallipoli Landings & ANZAC Mobilisation Enquiry 3

British, French, Indian, and Australian/New Zealand (ANZAC) forces land on the Gallipoli peninsula to knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war; eight months of bloody stalemate forge Australian national consciousness.

1 July 1916 • The First Day on the Somme & Destruction of the Pals Enquiry 2

Following a seven-day artillery bombardment, 100,000 British infantry assault intact German wire; 19,240 men are killed in hours, devastating entire towns and wiping out civic volunteer battalions.

September 1916 • First Tank Deployment at Flers-Courcelette Enquiry 2

Britain unveils the Mark I tank on the Somme, driving over trenches and crushing barbed wire; while mechanically unreliable, it inaugurates modern combined-arms armoured warfare.

8/16 Centrefold timeline: Dual-coding sketches and dates turns narrative history into permanent long-term memory.

Living Timeline • Part 2: Conscription, Total War & The Flawed Peace (1916–1923)

Living Timeline Dual-Coding Protocol: Complete each milestone sketchpad using dual-coding (combining visual storytelling symbols, causal arrows, and dates) to master the chronological spine across the centre-fold.
1916–1917 • Conscription, "Canary Girls" & Total War Mobilisation Enquiry 4

Parliament enforces military conscription for all eligible men while 1 million women enter munitions factories ("Canary Girls") and transport; German U-boat attacks bring Britain within weeks of starvation.

1917–1918 • Global Empire Mobilisation & 4 Million Troops Enquiry 3

Over 1.5 million Indian soldiers and hundreds of thousands of African, Caribbean, and Dominion troops fight across Europe, Africa, and the Middle East, sustaining the Allied war effort.

11 November 1918 • The Hundred Days Offensive & Armistice Enquiry 5

Allied combined-arms offensives break the Hindenburg Line; facing revolution and starvation at home, Germany signs the Armistice in Marshal Foch’s railway carriage, ending active combat.

28 June 1919 • The Signing of the Treaty of Versailles Enquiry 5

In the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, Allied powers force Germany to accept Article 231 (War Guilt), pay £6.6 billion in reparations, and surrender 13% of its European territory, creating a fragile peace.

Between 1914 and 1919, the Great War destroyed historic empires and fundamentally remade the political map of Europe. 9/16

ENQUIRY 5 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 9 • THE GREAT WAR: 1914–1919

Did the Treaty of Versailles solve the problems of 1914, or create the nightmares of 1939?

Core Specification Focus: Armistice of 11 November 1918; Paris Peace Conference; Big Three conflicting aims (Clemenceau, Lloyd George, Wilson); terms of the Treaty of Versailles (GARGLE: Article 231 War Guilt, £6.6bn reparations, military caps, Polish Corridor, Rhineland demilitarisation); Keynes’ "Carthaginian Peace" warning; Will Dyson’s "1940 Class" cartoon; League of Nations creation; modern revisionist debate on Allied enforcement.

12/16 Marshal Ferdinand Foch famously declared of the Treaty of Versailles: ‘This is not peace. It is an armistice for twenty years.’ Exactly twenty years later, in 1939, World War II began.

Key Stage 3 History Assessment Pathways • Level Descriptors & Criteria YEAR 9 STANDARDS
Emerging (1–2)
Recalls key facts of the Great War; describes basic trench conditions and Home Front changes using guided starters.

Emerging+ (3)
Identifies reasons for events; begins to explain why men volunteered, how tactics evolved, and why peace proved fragile.

Expected (4–5)
Explains multiple causes and consequences; writes structured causal paragraphs on Haig, Empire mobilization, and Versailles.

Expected+ (6–7)
Analyses historical significance; evaluates competing historical interpretations (Haig, Empire memory) with detailed primary evidence.
Focus: Sustained historiographical criteria.
Greater Depth (8–9)
Sustained, nuanced evaluative judgements; synthesises total war mobilization, geopolitical consequence, and modern historical legacies.
Focus: Nuanced synoptic judgements.
